title: Sakana AI and UC Berkeley release MASS, one model running its own agent team
subtitle: The method assigns one open-weights 27B model every role in its training loop — solver, workflow optimizer, evaluator — and reports score-per-token gains of 1.2–1.6x on research benchmarks.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Sakana AI and UC Berkeley released a paper and open-source implementation of MASS — Multi-Agent Self-Supervision — a self-improvement method in which a single language model plays every role in its own training loop. One copy of the model solves tasks, another revises the agent workflow, a third evaluates the results, and a fourth is fine-tuned on the preferred trajectories. The code is on GitHub under the SakanaAI organization.

The method is a response to a specific failure mode of self-improvement. On open-ended research problems — the kind without unit tests or gold answers — a model scoring its own work tends to propagate its own errors, and gains plateau or reverse within a few cycles. MASS splits the loop across coordinated subagents and treats the workflow itself as something to optimize, so the training signal comes from how a team of copies collaborates rather than from any one copy marking its own homework.

On four research benchmarks, two training cycles on Qwen3.6-27B improved score per output token by roughly 1.2x to 1.6x without an external teacher or human labels, according to Sakana's write-up. Ablations reportedly point to the workflow optimizer, not the evaluator, as the main bottleneck for how fast self-improvement runs. Training only on task-solving data also appears to transfer to the optimizer and evaluator roles, which hints at a cleaner data recipe than full-stack synthetic labeling.

A takeaway for learners: multi-agent systems are starting to behave less like orchestrations of different models and more like one model talking to itself in structured ways. If you want to work in this area, read the MASS code before the paper. The pipeline — workflow improvement, then post-training — is the shape most self-improvement research will take next, and reproducing it on a smaller open-weights model is a weekend-sized project with real resume value.
